beliefs.practice: Keep the cluster connection string and any credentials out of source control: read DOCUMENTDB_URI (and any user/password) from environment variables or a secrets store (e.g., Azure Key Vault) and provide a .env.example placeholder instead of real values.

Always connect with TLS/SSL enabled and verify server certificates (do not disable certificate validation) when creating the MongoDB-compatible client (e.g., pass tls=true/tlsCAFile or equivalent driver options).

Use the official MongoDB-compatible Python driver (pymongo or a MongoDB 7.0-compatible driver) and instantiate a single MongoClient per process that is reused across threads/requests instead of creating a client per request.
Tune client connection-pool options (e.g., maxPoolSize, minPoolSize, socketTimeoutMS, connectTimeoutMS) appropriate to your concurrency and keep long-lived clients rather than frequent reconnects.
Implement exponential-backoff retries for transient errors (connection/network timeouts, rate-limited responses); classify errors and avoid retrying on non-idempotent failures without safeguards.

Use a consistent, explicit schema for fraud documents: include fields transaction_id, account_id, timestamp, features (raw), embedding (fixed-length float32 array), embedding_dim, label (fraud/clean), and any indexed metadata; store embedding in its own field (e.g., embedding_vector).

Ensure all embeddings are the same dimension and record the dimension in each document or collection metadata; if using cosine similarity, pre-normalize vectors to unit length before storing to simplify query-time computation.

Index the vector field with an appropriate vector index and explicit parameters: declare vector dimension, metric (cosine or L2), and algorithm-specific settings (e.g., for IVF set nlist; for HNSW set M and efConstruction). Verify the index exists and its parameters before use.

Tune search-time ANN parameters (e.g., efSearch, probe/nprobe, or topK) per workload: set a conservative topK (e.g., 10–50) and adjust ef/probe to trade recall vs latency; avoid full-table scans in production.

Combine vector similarity with metadata filters (hybrid search) to restrict candidate sets before vector scoring: always apply transaction-date, account-id or other business filters when relevant to limit results and improve precision and cost.

Limit the size of documents and avoid embedding extremely large objects with vectors; keep embedding vectors lean (float32) and store large raw payloads or logs in a separate blob store with a reference in the document.

Use upserts or idempotent operations for seed and ingestion scripts (e.g., insert_one with upsert or replace_one with upsert) so repeated runs do not create duplicates and scripts can be safely re-run.
Avoid building large vector indexes in peak-production windows; build indexes in background or on a secondary replica and monitor index-build progress and resource usage.

Provision compute/throughput to match expected search and ingestion load (scale up cluster or choose appropriate compute tier such as M30) and measure RU or CPU usage; avoid under-provisioning index builds or heavy query patterns.
Use network security controls: restrict access with VNet/private endpoints or IP whitelists, and prefer private networking over public endpoints for production clusters.

Store and rotate credentials/key material with least privilege: prefer Azure AD-managed identities or Key Vault secrets and rotate keys regularly instead of baking long-lived secrets into apps or containers.
Do not log raw embeddings, transaction PII, or DB credentials in application logs; redact sensitive fields in any stored agent explanations or telemetry.
Benchmark vector search latency/recall for representative queries and capture metrics (p95 latency, recall@k, throughput); drive index and query parameter tuning from these benchmarks.
Version and store embedding-model metadata with each inserted vector (model name, model version, tokenizer options) so later re-embeddings or comparisons are auditable and consistent.

Use MongoDB sessions and transactions for multi-document atomic operations only if the cluster supports multi-document transactions and you need atomicity; otherwise design idempotent single-document writes.
Use TTL indexes for ephemeral data such as temporary caches, short-lived explanations, or staging inserts to automatically reclaim storage (create index on a datetime field with expireAfterSeconds).
Limit topK and post-filter search results in the app logic: compute a fraud risk score from a small set of nearest neighbors (e.g., top 10) and avoid returning or scoring on very large neighbor sets.

Persist provenance for model or agent decisions: store which embedding version and which documents matched (ids and distances) alongside the fraud risk score and explanation so results are reproducible and auditable.
Plan for backups and restores: ensure point-in-time restore or scheduled backups are enabled for production clusters and test restore procedures for the collection storing vectors and metadata.

When designing partition/shard keys for scale, choose keys that avoid hot partitions (e.g., hashed account_id or tenant id) and ensure vectors and their metadata that are queried together land in the same logical partition where possible.
